passage: The rain hammered the tin roof of the school hall, so the inter-house match was squeezed inside and everyone was packed shoulder to shoulder. When Chinmay's team missed a goal, someone near Thomas started to boo, and a few others joined in. Thomas felt the sound pull at him. Then he saw Chinmay by the goal post, staring at the floor with his jaw tight. Thomas kept his mouth shut. When Chinmay's team scored later, Thomas cheered loudly and clapped the goalkeeper, who grinned. Nobody could hear each other, but Chinmay looked up and found him in the crowd.

qa.q: Why was the match played inside the school hall?
qa.a: Because rain was hammering the roof.

qa.q: What was Thomas thinking when the booing started around him?
qa.a: He felt tempted to join in, but seeing Chinmay stare at the floor with a tight jaw made him think about how the booing landed on his friend.

qa.q: What did Thomas do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: He stayed quiet during the booing and cheered for a good play later, which showed friendly support without piling onto someone who was already upset.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt about the booing, compared with the cheering?
qa.a: The booing probably felt like jeering and added to his disappointment, while the cheer showed him someone was on his side.

grounding: A pupil hears booing and cheering at a match, considers the target's feelings and chooses not to join the jeering.

passage: “Booo!” The whole row of Class 6 yelled when Ishita walked out to bowl at the colony cricket day, and Aditi yelled too, laughing. But Ishita only bowed dramatically, and her team roared. Then the next over, Ishita's ball went wide and the booing grew louder and sharper. Aditi stopped. “Wait, that sounded different,” she whispered to her friend. Ishita's grin had gone stiff and she kept smoothing the ball on her shirt. Aditi walked to the boundary rope and called, “Come on, Ishita, you've got this!” 👏 Ishita glanced over and gave a small wave.

qa.q: Who did Aditi call out to from the boundary rope?
qa.a: Ishita.

qa.q: What did Aditi notice that made her stop booing?
qa.a: She heard the second round of booing as sharper and saw that Ishita's grin had gone stiff, so she thought it might no longer feel like friendly teasing.

qa.q: What could Aditi's friend do after hearing her whisper?
qa.a: The friend could join Aditi in cheering and choose friendly noise, since the same booing can be play one minute and hurtful the next.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt about the booing in the first over and the second?
qa.a: In the first over she played along as friendly rivalry, but by the second her stiff grin and fussing with the ball suggest it felt like pressure. 😔

grounding: Booing can be friendly rivalry or unkind jeering, and a child considers the target's feelings before joining in.

passage: “Boooo! Butterfingers!” Santosh cupped his hands and yelled as the Green House goalkeeper let in another goal. Around them, the Red House kids joined in. Kavitha tugged his sleeve. “Santosh. Look at him.” “What? It's just a house match. They booed us last year.” “That was at the captains, and they were laughing too. Look.” The goalkeeper, a small Class 4 boy, stood with his gloves over his face. His knees were shaking. Santosh lowered his hands. “Oh.” “Cheer our team instead,” said Kavitha. Santosh thought, then shouted, “Well played, Red House! And good try, keeper!” A couple of kids looked at him oddly. The goalkeeper looked up.

qa.q: Which house was the goalkeeper from?
qa.a: The goalkeeper was from Green House.

qa.q: What was Santosh feeling when he lowered his hands?
qa.a: Santosh felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising the booing was hurting a small, shaking boy.

qa.q: What did Kavitha suggest, and why was it better?
qa.a: She suggested cheering their own team instead, which kept the fun of rivalry without jeering at one scared player.

qa.q: What was the match like for the goalkeeper?
qa.a: The small goalkeeper was humiliated and shaking, hiding his face as the crowd booed each goal.

grounding: Shows booing that was friendly rivalry once turning into unkind jeering, and a child considering the target's feelings before joining in.

passage: I'm Ishita. At sports day last year, my friend Ganga was on the balance beam, and our whole class started chanting, “Cartwheel! Cartwheel! Cartwheel!” I was loudest. I thought we were helping. Ganga had told me that morning she wasn't sure about the cartwheel on the beam. She stood at the end with her arms out, and I saw her lip wobble. She did a small jump instead, and some kids went “Awww.” Afterwards she said, “You all made it so much harder.” I felt terrible. Now I cheer after someone finishes, not before, and I don't chant what I want them to do.

qa.q: What was the class chanting?
qa.a: They were chanting “Cartwheel! Cartwheel! Cartwheel!”

qa.q: How did Ishita feel after Ganga spoke?
qa.a: Ishita felt terrible, realising the cheering had pressured Ganga instead of helping.

qa.q: What did Ishita change, and why is it kinder?
qa.a: Ishita now cheers after someone finishes and doesn't chant demands, so the cheering supports rather than pressures.

qa.q: What was the balance beam like for Ganga with the chanting?
qa.a: Ganga felt pressured and scared, with the whole class demanding a move she wasn't sure about.

grounding: Shows group cheering putting pressure on a performer, and a child learning to consider the target's feelings before joining in.

passage: Quiz note, Friday. Deepika, Class 6. Today's inter-section quiz went well until the last round. When I made a terrible pun, Yash started a friendly “Boooo!” and the whole hall laughed, me included. That kind of boo is fun; everyone's in on it. But two minutes later, when Section C's youngest player got an easy question wrong, the booing started again, aimed at her. She shrank in her chair. Yash, I noticed, stopped at once and looked around. I paused the quiz and said, “Booing my jokes is fine. Booing a person who's trying is not.” After the quiz I spoke to the group who had kept going.

qa.q: What made the hall start a friendly boo?
qa.a: The teacher's terrible pun made Yash start a friendly “Boooo!”.

qa.q: What was the youngest player feeling when she shrank in her chair?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and hurt by the booing aimed at her after an easy mistake.

qa.q: How did Deepika make the difference between the two boos clear?
qa.a: Deepika paused the quiz and said booing her jokes is fine but booing a person who's trying is not, then spoke to the group afterwards.

qa.q: What might Yash have noticed that made the booing stop for Yash?
qa.a: Yash likely saw the young player shrink and realised this boo was aimed at a person, not a joke.

grounding: Shows booing as friendly fun in one moment and unkind jeering in the next, and considering the target's feelings.

passage:
Friday

Inter-house football final today, Green House against us. At the start, when Green came out, we all booed in a jokey way, "Boooo!", and they booed us back and everybody laughed. That felt fine.

But in the second half their goalkeeper, Disha, let one slip under her, and some Class 8 boys started shouting "Butterfingers! Loser!" and wouldn't stop. Disha's face crumpled. That wasn't friendly any more. I stopped booing.

Then we got a penalty, and everyone chanted my name, "GUR-LEEN! GUR-LEEN!" My legs went to jelly. I didn't want to take it, but I couldn't say no with all that noise. I missed. Nobody booed me, at least.

Gurleen

qa.q: What were the Class 8 boys shouting at Disha?
qa.a: "Butterfingers! Loser!"

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when everyone chanted the name for the penalty?
qa.a: Nervous and pressured, with legs like jelly, not wanting to take the penalty but unable to say no in all that noise.

qa.q: What did Gurleen do that was wise when the booing turned nasty?
qa.a: Gurleen stopped booing once it became jeering at a hurt person rather than a shared joke between rival houses.

qa.q: How might Disha have felt when the boys kept shouting?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt, as her crumpling face shows; for her it was no longer friendly rivalry.

grounding: It is a child's diary about booing as friendly rivalry turning into jeering, and cheering becoming pressure, with thought for how the target feels.
